name: Parc Monceau
short_description: Romantic English-style public park in the 8th arrondissement, created in 1778 and famous for its scattered architectural follies including a Roman colonnade and miniature Egyptian pyramid.

beats.script_body: Marcel Proust (1871–1922) lived nearby and played in Parc Monceau as a child. The park is said not to have changed much since then — more than a century later still showing off Paris on her most refined behavior. In the air of June, among the roses and gardenia trees in blossom, carry the memory of Manet, Gounod, Debussy, Fauré, Dumas fils, and Rostand, who all worked or lived in the Monceau neighborhood. Today the streets and mansions of the eighth arrondissement that border the park cast a spell of a certain Parisian past — exclusive, privileged.

Statues of Chopin, Musset, and Maupassant set into flower beds on sloping lawns

beats.source_passage: Wandering through Monceau, past the classical colonnade, the oval lake, lily ponds, rock gardens, the statues of Chopin, Musset, and Maupassant set into lovely flower beds and sloping lawns, you feel part of this legacy. In June, the roses and gardenia trees in blossom, the air carries the memory of Manet, Gounod, Debussy, Faure, Dumas fils, and Rostand, who all worked or lived in the Monceau neighborhood. Today, the streets and mansions of the eighth arrondissement that border the park cast a spell of a certain Parisian past, exclusive, privileged. Marcel Proust (1871—1922), who lived nearby, played here as a child; the park is said not to have changed much since then, more than a century later still showing off Paris on her most refined behavior.

fact_check.notes: Proust born 1871, died 1922, lived at 45 rue de Courcelles and 9 boulevard Malesherbes near the park — well-established biographical fact. Artist residents of the Monceau neighborhood are consistently cited in multiple Paris guidebook sources.

beats.script_body: In her 1901 novel Claudine in Paris, Colette plays with the contradiction between the Monceau neighborhood's reputation for good taste and a brutal reality. Claudine is drawn to the green park — its soft lawns veiled in misty curtains of spray, enchanting trees, warm dampness — but the next moment she spots Luce, her best friend from childhood, strolling through. An innocent country girl when she ran away to Paris, Luce is now a kept woman, a prostitute, who lives nearby in opulence and servitude in the rue de Courcelles. Revolted by the love of money and the fake respectability that the Monceau quartier exhales, Colette (as Claudine) realizes her old friend is now a spiritual ruin, her luxurious clothes a sad disguise.
key_claims: Colette's Claudine in Paris (1901) is set partly in and around Parc Monceau
The novel contrasts the neighborhood's reputation for good taste with a kept woman's sad reality
beats.source_passage: In fiction, Monceau loses its civilized veneer, at times becoming a menacing backdrop. In her novel Claudine in Paris (1901), Colette plays with the contradiction between the neighborhood's reputation of good taste and the brutal reality: 'The green Parc Monceau, with its soft lawns veiled in misty curtains of spray from the sprinkler, attracted me, like something good to eat. There were fewer children there than in the Luxembourg. It was better altogether. But those lawns that are swept like floors! Never mind, the trees enchanted me and the warm dampness I breathed in relaxed me . . . that sound of leaves, how sweet it was.' But the next moment she spots Luce, her best friend from childhood, strolling through the park. An innocent country girl when she ran away to Paris, Luce is now a kept woman, a prostitute, who lives nearby in opulence and servitude in the rue de Courcelles. Revolted by the love of money and the fake respectability that the Monceau quartier exhales, Colette (Claudine) realizes her old friend is now a spiritual ruin, her luxurious clothes a sad disguise.

fact_check.notes: Claudine in Paris published 1901 under Willy's name, authored by Colette — well documented. The Luce/kept-woman subplot is accurately summarized from the source.

beats.script_body: In the 2006 thriller Ne le dis à personne (Tell No One), a desperate Francis Cluzet sits on a bench just inside the wrought-iron and golden Courcelles entrance — next to the children's play area and kiosk — waiting for his wife, who may or may not have been brutally murdered. The film's denouement implicates the powerful class at home in this quartier, their politesse masking a ruthless corruption. Director Jean-Pierre Melville's masterpiece L'armée des ombres (Army of Shadows, 1969) — based on his own years in the Resistance and on Joseph Kessel's novel — ends with the tragic murder of the Résistante Mathilde (Simone Signoret) against the backdrop of those same high iron gates of the Courcelles entrance. The Champs-Elysées and quartiers north of it, including Monceau, were known during World War II as collaborationist territory, dangerous ground for Résistants like Melville, who in the film was captured by the SS near the Arc de Triomphe.

beats.script_body: The land beneath Parc Monceau started out as the twelfth-century village of Monceau. Joan of Arc made her camp here in the fifteenth century. The park itself was designed as an English garden in the eighteenth century, then acquired a Scottish gardener; the omnipresent Alphand continued the Anglicization in the nineteenth century. So despite its reputation as the height of French refinement, the park's DNA is decidedly Anglo-Scottish.

short_description: Second Empire mansion built 1869–1875 by architect Henri Parent for banker Édouard André and painter Nélie Jacquemart, opened as a museum in 1913 with their Italian Renaissance and 18th-century French collection.

name: Musée de la Vie Romantique

beats.script_body: At the top of the lane leading to the house at 16 rue Chaptal, the garden opens on your right, in the shade of huge old chestnut trees, bordered with bushes of bright flowers. Sometimes there's the sound of quiet conversation among visitors seated at small tables, enjoying the fare of the café. It is not as loud as the singing of the birds nesting in the magisterial chestnuts. The city feels far away; this hidden corner of the ninth arrondissement feels out of time, bringing to mind the less cacophonous era of the people who made this place famous.

beats.script_body: In the years 1838 to 1847, the lovers Frédéric Chopin and George Sand — born Aurore Dupin Dudevant — and their friend Eugène Delacroix used to visit their friend and neighbor Ary Scheffer, the painter who lived here and worked in the upstairs studio of this house. Sand was a prolific and bold novelist who denounced marriage as 'one of the most barbaric institutions society has engendered' and wrote frankly about female sexual desire and pleasure. Chopin, her 'divine' pianist and composer from Poland, she called her 'angel' and nicknamed 'Chip Chip.' His music brought her to ecstasy. Passionately devoted to the woman he knew as lover, friend, mother, muse, nurse, manager, and fellow artist, Chopin called her l'Aurore — his dawn. Delacroix, often accompanied by his cat named Cupid, painted a double portrait of them. But after their mutual disenchantment in 1847, the former lovers moved away from this neighborhood. With the failure of romantic love — the loss of trust, the suspicions and resentments — Sand and Chopin became estranged. Alone, sick, and heartbroken, Chopin died two years later, in 1849. Although this tragic end hardly resonates in Scheffer's garden, the dynamic duo of love and death, joy and pain that figure in their story correspond to the pattern of the seasons: the heat of summer becoming — inevitably — the ice of winter.

beats.source_passage: Sitting here, away from the noise of the streets, you find yourself imagining the nineteenth century, the years 1838—1847, say, when the lovers Frederic Chopin and George Sand (the pen name of Aurore Dupin Dudevant) and their friend Eugene Delacroix used to visit their friend and neighbor Ary Scheffer, the painter who lived here and worked in the upstairs studio of this house. The tranquillity of the scene is only a partial evocation of la vie romantique, which this garden and house commemorate. Its natural beauty and calm make the perfect backdrop for the story of happy lovers, one a prolific and bold novelist—Sand wrote about the sexual desires and pleasure of women, denounced marriage as 'one of the most barbaric institutions society has engendered'—the other a genius, a 'divine' pianist and composer who came from Poland. Sand called Chopin her 'angel' and nicknamed him 'Chip Chip.' His music brought her to ecstasy. Passionately devoted to the woman he knew as lover, friend, mother, muse, nurse, manager, and fellow artist, Chopin called her l'nsAurore, his dawn. Delacroix, often accompanied by his cat who was named Cupid, painted a double portrait of them. But after their mutual disenchantment in 1847, the former lovers moved away from this neighborhood. With the failure of romantic love—the loss of trust, the suspicions and resentments—Sand and Chopin became estranged. Alone, sick, and heartbroken, Chopin died two years later, in 1849.

fact_check.notes: All biographical facts (Chopin/Sand relationship 1838–1847, Sand's birth name Aurore Dupin Dudevant, Delacroix double portrait, Chopin death 1849) are well-established. Ary Scheffer's address at rue Chaptal confirmed.

name: Square des Batignolles

beats.script_body: Square des Batignolles has known many incarnations. Originally the site of a warehouse of demolition materials when the hamlet of Batignolles was outside the city limits, it became a public space in 1835 — La Place de la Promenade — where village festivals and holidays were celebrated. After 1860, when the village became part of Paris, Napoleon III gave the job of transforming it to his genius landscape architect Jean-Charles Adolphe Alphand. Over the next ten years Alphand would redesign and Anglicize twenty-four gardens and parks across the city — among them Parc Monceau, Parc des Buttes-Chaumont, the Bois de Boulogne, and the Bois de Vincennes — giving each its English-style grottoes, cascades, and miniature lakes.

beats.source_passage: Like so many Parisian squares, Batignolles has known many incarnations. Originally the site of a warehouse of demolition materials when the hamlet of Batignolles was outside the city limits, it became a public space in 1835—La Place de la Promenade—where village festivals and holidays were celebrated. After 1860, when the village became part of the city, Napoleon III, as part of his project to make such spaces into English-style squares—with grottoes and cascades and miniature lakes—gave the job of transforming Batignolles to his genius landscape architect, Jean-Charles Adolphe Alphand. Over the next ten years, Alphand would redesign—Anglicize—twenty-four gardens and parks in all.

fact_check.notes: Alphand's role under Napoleon III redesigning Parisian parks is a well-documented historical fact. The 1860 annexation of suburban communes including Batignolles is confirmed.

beats.script_body: Near the grotto, a sculpted bust of nineteenth-century poet Léon Dierx commemorates the associations of this quartier with the many artists who lived and worked in the surrounding streets and boulevards. Manet, Courbet, and Degas — sometime members of the groupe des Batignolles — painted scenes of café and opera house nightlife; Manet captured the poetry of the new nearby railroad station in La Gare Saint-Lazare. Mallarmé, Leconte de Lisle, and Paul Verlaine (1844–1896) attended the same literary salons, though de Lisle and Verlaine came to detest each other.

beats.script_body: Verlaine moved with his parents to the Batignolles village as a child and grew up to be considered the 'prince of poets' by his peers and an immoral social outcast by bourgeois society. He took part in the Paris Commune, abandoned his wife and child for the poet Arthur Rimbaud, did time in prison for attempting to murder Rimbaud, converted to Catholicism, and killed himself with a steady diet of absinthe and beer. He is buried in the nearby Batignolles Cemetery, and a piece of his writing — Christ en Croix — is affixed to a wall in the Église Sainte-Marie des Batignolles, just across the tree-lined Place du Docteur Félix Lobligeois (with a Wallace fountain in good working order). A statue of Verlaine — called a 'ragamuffin angel' and 'an inspired derelict' — stands in the Luxembourg Gardens, in tribute to his poetry: 'grey and sad and cool and deep and unlike anything else in the world.' On a moody wet November day in the soundless stir of the chestnuts of the square, you hear Verlaine's music — 'the silence of eternity.' He wrote: Il pleure dans mon coeur / Comme il pleut sur la ville — 'It weeps in my heart / As it rains on the city.'

beats.script_body: The square is especially appealing in bad weather — 'bad' meaning light misting rain, low clouds of bright silver-gray. People sit on benches, some chatting, others fixed in solitary silence, not an umbrella or a smile in sight. The stately chestnut trees, old beautiful presences, breathe in, breathe out — a generous high ceiling of shelter and shade. Baudelaire made poetry out of the city's moody 'great gray sky,' its 'mists and rains.' Enter from place Charles-Fillion or rue Cardinet, metro Brochant.

name: Square d'Orléans

beats.script_body: Through the entrance at 80 rue Taitbout (open weekdays), Square d'Orléans was called 'a bright and music-filled utopia of artists' — a gracious Regency-London-style complex built in 1829 that was the residential heart of La Nouvelle Athènes, the expensive district where Romantic-era artists gathered. Chopin and Sand lived together here from 1842 to 1847. For appearances, Chopin leased the ground floor of no. 9; Sand and her children lived at no. 5, near the cobblestoned carriage entrance. The lovers entertained Balzac, the singer Pauline Viardot (lover of Turgenev), the Polish poet Adam Mickiewicz, along with Delacroix, Dumas fils, and Heinrich Heine. Today, the courtyard's large fountain waters the magnolia tree of the square's private gardens.

key_claims: Square d'Orléans entered at 80 rue Taitbout, open weekdays
Built in 1829, modeled on Regency London architecture
Residential center of La Nouvelle Athènes
Chopin (no. 9) and Sand (no. 5) lived together here 1842–1847
Regular visitors included Balzac, Pauline Viardot, Turgenev, Adam Mickiewicz, Delacroix, Dumas fils, Heinrich Heine
beats.source_passage: Walk down rue Saint-Georges, turn right into rue Saint-Lazare, then, at the post office, take another right to 80, rue Taitbout. Here is the entrance to Square d'Orleans (open weekdays). A 'bright and music-filled utopia of artists,' in the words of Benita Eisler, where Chopin and Sand lived together from 1842 to 1843, though for the sake of appearance Chopin leased the ground floor of number 9, Sand and her children number 5 near the cobblestoned carriage entrance. Built in 1829, the gracious complex, modeled on the architecture of Regency London, was the residential center of La Nouvelle Athenes, the expensive district that was home to many romantic artists. Here the lovers entertained Balzac; the singer Pauline Viardot, lover of Turgenev; the Polish poet Adam Mickiewicz; as well as Delacroix, Dumas fils, and Heinrich Heine. Today, the courtyard's large fountain, between Chopin and Sand's apartments, waters the magnolia tree of the square's private gardens.

opening_hours_basis: A gated private residential courtyard off rue Taitbout; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Private residential courtyard-square off a passage, a paved court with a fountain and elegant facades to walk into and round; nothing public to enter.
judgement_basis: A private residential courtyard-square off rue Taitbout entered through a carriage arch, with paved cobbled ground and no lawns for children to range freely, some benches and quiet enclosed surroundings good for talking, but it is a gated private enclave closed and unwelcoming to outsiders at night.
queue_basis: A private residential courtyard-garden you walk into through an open gate with no ticket or security, so there is no line to price.

name: Cathédrale Saint-Alexandre-Nevsky
short_description: Russian Orthodox cathedral consecrated in 1861, the first permanent Russian Orthodox place of worship in Paris, built in a Byzantine-Muscovite style with five gilded onion domes.

beats.script_body: The Russian Orthodox church at 12 rue Daru sits in the heart of Paris's Little Russia.
key_claims: The Russian Orthodox church at 12 rue Daru is the heart of Paris's Little Russia
beats.source_passage: CATHEDRALE SAINT-ALEXANDRE NEVSKY 12, rue Daru; Tues, Fri, Sun, 3—5. The Russian Orthodox church in the heart of Paris's Little Russia.

fact_check.notes: Cathedral at rue Daru confirmed as Russian Orthodox and the center of the Paris Russian émigré community.

opening_hours_basis: A church you enter with restricted visiting hours; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Russian Orthodox cathedral with five gilded onion domes; the exterior and forecourt reward a good look, and the icon-filled Byzantine-Muscovite interior takes around twenty minutes when open during limited visiting hours.
judgement_basis: A working Orthodox church where silence and reverence are expected, with no running and no casual public seating for conversation, and its doors and surrounding gates are closed after services so no one is left standing inside after dark.
queue_basis: A working Orthodox cathedral with restricted visiting hours entered through one door; a small line can form only within its limited opening windows and is otherwise negligible.

name: Place Saint-Georges
opening_hours_basis: An open public square with a central monument viewed from the pavement, never closed off.
visit_basis: Small ornate 19th-century circle with a central monument and townhouse facades around it; you walk the ring reading the buildings, nothing to enter.
judgement_basis: A traffic circle around a central fountain with roads on all sides, so a child could run into vehicles and there is no protected play space, the narrow central island has little usable free seating and traffic noise makes talking effort, but it is lit, open and busy with people and traffic after dark.
queue_basis: An open public square with no door and no interior; the whole value stands in the open, so there is nothing to queue for.
